# Writing in English as a second language

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Learning objectives
By the end of this chapter you will be able to:

- recognise the two sources of second-language difficulty
- correct common first-language transfer patterns in English prose
- use language-editing tools without losing your voice
:::

Most health researchers publish in English regardless of the language they think in, dream in, and use to argue with their supervisors. This is not a disadvantage to be overcome; it is the condition of contemporary science. The researchers who handle it best are not those who write perfect English; they are those who have learned to separate the two distinct problems: saying what you mean, and saying it in English.

These are not the same problem, and they have different remedies.

## The two sources of difficulty

When an L2 writer produces an unclear sentence, the cause is usually one of two things. Either the argument is not yet clear enough to be written in any language — the problem is thinking, not translation — or the argument is clear but the English is getting in the way. The first problem requires more thinking; the second requires language help. Misdiagnosing the source wastes time. Before asking an editor or a tool to fix a sentence, ask whether you can state the sentence in Portuguese in a way you are satisfied with. If you cannot, fix the thinking first. If you can, the problem is the translation.

## Over-hedging in L2

The most consistent writing pattern I observe in L2 health researchers is over-hedging. The scientific caution is often real: observational studies warrant hedges, association is not causation, single-centre findings should not be generalised. But L2 writers hedge for an additional reason that has nothing to do with the data: linguistic caution. When you are not confident in your English, qualifying everything feels safer. The result is prose that systematically understates findings the data actually support.

The diagnostic question is the same as for native writers: if you removed the hedge, would the claim still be accurate? If yes, the hedge is linguistic, not scientific, and should come out. A finding supported by an adjusted HR of 1.31 with a 95% CI that excludes 1 does not need "might perhaps suggest a possible trend toward".

::: {.column-margin}
The hedging section of [clear writing](03-clear-writing.qmd) gives a calibration exercise using three versions of the same finding — unhedged, appropriate, and over-hedged. The over-hedged version is a reliable portrait of the default L2 first draft. The appropriate version is the target.
:::

## Common Portuguese-to-English patterns

Some transfer errors from Portuguese are grammatically legal in English and therefore survive copyediting. A native-speaker reviewer will read them as non-native; some will be flagged; many will not. The most common in clinical health writing:

**Direct transfer of verb constructions.** *"The study allowed to conclude"* (o estudo permitiu concluir) is grammatically wrong in English; the correct form is *"the study allowed us to conclude"*, or more cleanly, *"the study showed"*. *"It was evidenced that"* (evidenciou-se que) translates to *"we found that"* or *"the results showed that"*. *"It was verified that"* (verificou-se que) → *"we found"* or *"we observed"*.

**False cognates.** *"Actual"* in English means real or existing; Portuguese *actual* means current. Write *"current guidelines"*, not *"actual guidelines"*. *"Eventually"* in English means at some unspecified future time; Portuguese *eventualmente* means possibly. *"Proper"* in English means appropriate; Portuguese *próprio* can mean own. These errors survive because they are not errors in English — they are just the wrong word.

**Register imports.** *"In what concerns"* (no que diz respeito a) → *"regarding"* or *"for"*. *"Under the point of view of"* → *"from the perspective of"* or simply *"for"*. *"The majority of"* is correct but often heavy; *"most"* is usually cleaner. *"In the present study"* is a formality imported from Portuguese academic register; in English biomedical prose, *"in this study"* or *"here"* is more natural.

**Preposition errors.** Portuguese uses *em* for relationships that English covers with *in*, *on*, *at*, and *by*. These errors are the most resistant to self-correction because they feel invisible. *"The patients were admitted in the hospital"* → *"admitted to the hospital"*. *"Enrolled in the study since 2018"* → *"enrolled from 2018"* or *"enrolled between 2018 and 2023"*.

::: {.column-margin}
Keep a personal list of the constructions you reach for in Portuguese and their English equivalents. A reference of twenty to thirty phrases built from your own errors — not a generic style guide — is the most effective L2 editing tool available, because it is calibrated to your specific patterns.
:::

## Common Mandarin-to-English patterns

The patterns below are the most common in published clinical research submissions from Mandarin L1 speakers. Identify your own list in revision; these are starting points, not a complete inventory.

**Topic-prominence constructions.** Mandarin is a topic-prominent language: it is natural to front-load the sentence with a topic frame before the main predicate. *"As for the patients with LVEF below 40%, their readmission rate was higher"* → *"Patients with LVEF below 40% had a higher readmission rate."* The topic frame adds no information the predicate does not already carry.

**Article omission.** Mandarin has no grammatical articles. The most consistent error is the missing definite article before noun phrases already established in context. *"Patient was admitted to hospital"* → *"The patient was admitted to hospital."* *"Result showed that"* → *"The result showed that."* This error is easy to miss in self-editing because it is invisible to the writer.

**Tense inconsistency.** Mandarin encodes time through adverbs and context rather than verb morphology. In English clinical writing, completed actions are past tense. The abstract, methods, and results are in past tense; the introduction and discussion may use present tense for established facts. Mixing tenses within a section — often defaulting to present — is a common signal of L1 Mandarin transfer.

**Stacked noun modifiers.** Mandarin allows long noun-noun compounds that are grammatical but dense in English. *"NT-proBNP discharge level prediction model accuracy"* → *"the accuracy of the NT-proBNP-based discharge prediction model"*. Use prepositions to break the stack.

## Common Spanish-to-English patterns

The patterns below are the most common in published clinical research submissions from Spanish L1 speakers. The overlap with Portuguese is partial; the differences matter.

**False cognates (Spanish-specific set).** *Realizar* means to carry out or conduct, not to realise. *"We realized a clinical trial"* → *"We conducted a clinical trial."* *Evidenciar* means to show or demonstrate, not to evidence: *"the results evidenced that"* → *"the results showed that."* *Actual* and *eventually* share the same trap as in Portuguese (current and possibly, not real and finally).

*Se* **constructions.** Spanish uses reflexive *se* for impersonal constructions that English renders with passive or active voice. *"Se observó que"* → *"We observed that"* or *"It was observed that"* (not *"It was observed itself that"*). *"Se excluyeron los pacientes"* → *"Patients were excluded"* (not *"Patients excluded themselves"*). Choose active voice where possible.

**Sentence length.** Spanish biomedical writing favours longer, more syntactically complex sentences than English. A Spanish methods sentence may carry three subordinate clauses and remain readable; the English version usually benefits from splitting. When a sentence in your translation runs past 35 words, look for a natural split point.

**Adjective-noun agreement.** Spanish adjectives agree in gender and number with the noun they modify. In translation, agreement errors sometimes persist: *"the patients were treated with the various protocols"* where *"various protocols"* translates *varios protocolos* without adjustment. These are usually minor but catch the eye of native readers.

## Using tools for L2 writing

The tier framework in the AI writing chapter applies, but with a calibration specific to L2 writers. For a native English speaker, Tier 1 (grammar and clarity editing on your own prose) is a minor convenience. For an L2 writer, it is closer to essential: a tool that catches preposition errors, agreement errors, and awkward transfer constructions is doing genuine work that would otherwise require a human language editor or extensive self-editing. Using a grammar tool or LLM for language revision of your own prose is not a shortcut to thinking; it is appropriate tool use for a real constraint.

Two limits apply. First, the tool applies the statistical norms of general written English, not the conventions of your field. Highly technical phrasing — *"adjusted for confounders by propensity score overlap weighting"* — may be flagged as unusual or rewritten to something generic. Accept language corrections; scrutinise content corrections. Second, the tool's output may pass for native-speaker English while subtly changing what you meant. Compare every rewritten sentence against your original to confirm the scientific claim is intact.

## Preserving your voice

The fear L2 writers most often express is losing their voice. In practice, L2 scientific writing has two separate voice problems: the personality of the prose (which tool revision can flatten) and the precision of the argument (which tool revision can distort). Protect both differently. For personality: revise the tool's output back toward your sentence rhythms; you are not obligated to accept every stylistic change. For precision: read the revised version as a scientist, not as a writer, and check every claim against your data.

Scientific prose is not where individual style does its most important work. What is most distinctively yours in a journal article is not the sentence rhythm; it is the question you chose to ask, the analytical decision you made, the limitation you were honest about when others would have glossed it. Those survive any language revision.

A practical note: if a sentence in English feels wrong, it usually is. Trust the discomfort. You may not be able to say why the sentence is wrong, but your reading-in-English accumulation is often a reliable detector even when it cannot articulate the problem. Write a note to yourself — *"recheck this sentence"* — and return to it after the draft is done, when you can compare it against the surrounding text and decide whether it needs a language editor's eye.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Practice: revise the L2 patterns

Each sentence shows a common second-language pattern. Revise it before revealing a suggested rewrite.

1. *"In this study, we tried to investigate the possible potential association that may exist between the biomarker and the outcome."*
2. *"The obtained results demonstrate clearly that the treatment is effective."*
3. *"It is well known that heart failure is a serious disease."*

---

Suggested rewrites:

1. **Stacked hedges and redundancy.** *"We examined the association between the biomarker and the outcome."* — "possible potential… that may exist" piles up three hedges, and "tried to investigate" weakens the claim before it is made.
2. **Over-claiming from one study, vague verb.** *"These results indicate that the treatment reduced [outcome] in this cohort."* — "demonstrate clearly" overstates what one study shows; name what improved.
3. **Empty opener.** Cut it, or replace with a specific cited fact: *"Heart failure causes more than one million hospital admissions a year in Europe [ref]."*
:::
